method: Live web search for 4 representative query families spanning the competitiveness spectrum found in Phase IV's research: two 'alternatives' head-terms for massive, market-leading SaaS brands (clickup, salesforce), one 'alternative' query for a mid-tier developer tool (n8n), and one comparison query for a niche/specialist product (umbraco vs wordpress). Structure and domain type recorded, not scraped content.

resultComposition: clickup.com/blog (the vendor itself, capturing its own churn-intent query)
clickup alternatives.domainTypeSummary: 100% of the observed results are either massive brands (Salesforce, ClickUp itself), a huge review/directory platform (G2), a dedicated alternatives directory (AlternativeTo), a high-authority editorial review site, or competing vendors' own content-marketing blogs. Zero independent third-party comparison sites of Miloosh's type and size.

salesforce alternatives.domainTypeSummary: Same pattern, with an even higher-authority media brand present (Forbes). Zero independent third-party comparison sites.

resultComposition: github.com/topics (a tag/topic aggregation page, not real competing content)
marketermilk.com/blog (a marketing-focused content site, adjacent but not a direct competitor)
n8n alternative.domainTypeSummary: No Salesforce/Forbes-level giants for this smaller, more specialized product -- but still dominated entirely by competing vendors' own content marketing plus the AlternativeTo directory. No independent third-party editorial sites at all.

umbraco vs wordpress.domainTypeSummary: COMPLETELY DIFFERENT competitive landscape: zero massive brands, zero vendor self-promotion (no umbraco.com or wordpress.com), zero major directories or media brands. The entire result set is small-to-mid digital agencies writing this as portfolio/expertise content -- a genuinely winnable competitive set for an independent site.

keyFinding: Query competitiveness varies enormously by how mainstream the base product is, not just by category or query type. 'Alternatives to [massive market-leading brand]' queries are structurally near-unwinnable for a new independent site regardless of content quality -- the SERP is occupied by the vendor itself, competing vendors' content-marketing budgets, massive media brands, and dedicated directories. Comparison queries for less-mainstream, more specialized products (like Umbraco, ~0.1% CMS market share) face dramatically weaker competition -- small agencies, not giants. This directly validates the Phase IV Umbraco intervention as strategically correct (a genuinely winnable query, not just a high-volume one), and gives a concrete prioritization rule for future waves: prioritize comparison-intent queries for specialist/niche products over alternatives-intent queries for household-name SaaS brands.
copyrightNote: No result page content was reproduced verbatim beyond what a normal search-results listing already discloses (title, domain, general topic) -- consistent with this session's standing copyright discipline.
